data.title: Café-au-lait macules — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 16 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Café-au-lait macules** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What are café-au-lait macules (CALMs)?**
- Well-defined, uniformly light- to dark-brown ('coffee with milk') macules/patches with smooth or irregular borders, present at birth or appearing in early childhood; increase in number and size with age in childhood
- 1–3 CALMs are common in normal population (10–25%)

**Q2. Histopathology.**
- Increased melanin in basal keratinocytes and melanocytes with normal or slightly increased melanocyte number; giant pigment granules (macromelanosomes) in some, especially NF1 (not specific)

**Q3. When are CALMs significant? Name associated syndromes.**
- ≥6 CALMs >5 mm prepubertal or >15 mm postpubertal suggest NF1
- NF1, NF2 (fewer CALMs), Legius syndrome (SPRED1 — CALMs + axillary freckling without neurofibromas), McCune–Albright syndrome (large unilateral jagged 'coast of Maine' CALMs following midline, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, precocious puberty — GNAS mosaic), constitutional mismatch repair deficiency, Noonan with multiple lentigines (LEOPARD), Fanconi anaemia, ataxia-telangiectasia, Bloom syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, Watson syndrome, Silver–Russell, ring chromosome syndromes
- Shape: smooth 'coast of California' border in NF1 vs jagged 'coast of Maine' in McCune–Albright

**Q4. Give the NIH diagnostic criteria for NF1 (revised 2021).**
- Two or more of: ≥6 CALMs (>5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal); freckling in axillary or inguinal region (Crowe's sign); ≥2 neurofibromas of any type or 1 plexiform neurofibroma; optic pathway glioma; ≥2 iris Lisch nodules or ≥2 choroidal abnormalities (on OCT/NIR imaging); distinctive osseous lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, anterolateral tibial bowing/pseudarthrosis); heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant
- In a child of an affected parent, one criterion is enough

**Q5. Write a short note on neurocutaneous syndromes (PYQ).**
- Phakomatoses — disorders of neuroectoderm with skin and CNS involvement: NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis complex, Sturge–Weber syndrome, von Hippel–Lindau, ataxia-telangiectasia, incontinentia pigmenti, hypomelanosis of Ito, neurocutaneous melanosis, PHACE, linear nevus sebaceous syndrome (Schimmelpenning)

**Q6. Differential diagnosis of CALMs.**
- Congenital melanocytic naevus (raised, hair, darker), nevus spilus (CALM-like background with dark speckles), Becker's naevus (shoulder, hair, after puberty), lentigines (smaller, darker), freckles (sun-dependent), post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, mastocytoma (Darier's sign), segmental pigmentation disorder

**Q7. Management.**
- Isolated CALMs — reassurance
- Multiple — full skin exam (freckling, neurofibromas), eye exam (Lisch nodules), BP, growth, development, family history; genetic testing; follow-up yearly for children at risk of NF1
- Cosmetic: Q-switched (Nd:YAG 532, ruby, alexandrite) or picosecond lasers — variable response, recurrence common; camouflage

**Q8. How many CALMs are normal?**
- 1–2 CALMs in ~25% of normal children; ≥3 in <1%; ≥6 typical CALMs raise strong suspicion of NF1 (≈ 80% of children with ≥6 develop NF1 if no family history after genetic testing — including Legius)

**Q9. What are 'typical' vs 'atypical' CALMs?**
- Typical (NF1): uniformly pigmented, oval, smooth borders, ≥0.5 cm
- Atypical: irregular jagged borders, variable pigmentation, segmental — suggests other syndromes (McCune–Albright, constitutional mismatch repair deficiency, ring chromosome) or isolated

**Q10. What is constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome (CMMRD)?**
- Biallelic MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2 mutations: CALMs (atypical), early childhood brain tumours, haematological malignancies, colorectal cancers; consanguinity; differentiate from NF1 by genetic testing and tumour risk

**Q11. What is the role of lasers and expected outcomes?**
- Q-switched 532/755/694 nm and picosecond lasers: variable clearance (~50%), recurrence common (up to 50% within months), irregular-bordered CALMs respond better; test patch first; risk of hyper/hypopigmentation

**Q12. Describe Watson syndrome and ring chromosome syndromes.**
- Watson: NF1 allelic — CALMs, pulmonary stenosis, short stature, intellectual disability
- Ring chromosome syndromes (ring 7, 11, 12, 15, 17): multiple CALMs with growth retardation and developmental delay

**Q13. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q14. Describe the other cutaneous features of NF1.**
- Axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign — appears 3–5 y), cutaneous neurofibromas (soft, 'button-hole' invagination, puberty onwards), plexiform neurofibromas ('bag of worms'; risk of MPNST), juvenile xanthogranulomas, naevus anaemicus, hypopigmented macules
- Treatment of symptomatic plexiform neurofibroma: selumetinib (MEK inhibitor)

**Q15. What are Lisch nodules?**
- Pigmented hamartomas of the iris (melanocytic) — dome-shaped yellow-brown elevations on slit-lamp; appear in childhood, present in >90% of adults with NF1; asymptomatic

**Q16. Describe McCune–Albright syndrome briefly.**
- Post-zygotic activating GNAS mutation: large segmental CALMs with jagged 'coast of Maine' border respecting midline, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (fractures, deformity), endocrine hyperfunction — precocious puberty (girls), hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, Cushing's, phosphate wasting

## Quick spotter facts
- ≥6 CALMs + axillary freckles — NF1
- Coast of California (NF1) vs coast of Maine (McCune–Albright)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hyperpigmentation; neurocutaneous syndromes); NIH 2021 revised NF1 criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
